title: Trading Costs & Electronic Markets
hook: Every trade leaks value through spreads, impact, and delay. Measure the full bill with implementation shortfall.

keyterms.def: Directly observable costs: commissions, exchange fees, taxes, and stamp duties paid to execute a trade.
Ask minus bid; the implicit cost of demanding immediacy. Half-spread is often used as the entry cost estimate.
2 x |trade price - midquote at order arrival|; a realized measure of the spread cost actually paid.
Adverse price movement caused by your own order (slippage); larger for big, urgent, or illiquid trades.
Value lost from price drift between the investment decision and the order reaching the market.
Difference between a hypothetical paper-portfolio return and the actual return; captures all explicit and implicit costs.
Volume-weighted average price over a period; a common execution benchmark for judging fill quality.
Same security trading across many venues (exchanges, ECNs, dark pools), splitting liquidity across the market.

body: Total trading cost is far larger than the commission line. It splits into explicit costs (commissions, fees, taxes) that appear on the confirmation, and implicit costs that must be estimated.

The main implicit costs are the bid-ask spread (paying the ask to buy, hitting the bid to sell), market impact where a large order pushes the price against you, and delay/opportunity cost from prices moving while the order is worked or from failing to fill at all.
Implicit costs dominate for large institutional orders and in illiquid names, so measuring them is the whole point of transaction cost analysis.
sections.formula: Effective spread = 2 x | Trade price - Midquote |

callout.label: IMPLICIT > EXPLICIT
callout.text: For institutional block trades, market impact and delay usually swamp commissions.

body: Implementation shortfall (IS) compares a paper portfolio (fill the whole order instantly at the decision price, no costs) with the real portfolio actually achieved. The gap is the total cost of implementing the idea.

IS decomposes into four pieces: explicit costs (commissions/fees), the realized profit/loss or execution cost (fill price vs decision price on shares traded), the delay cost (decision price vs price when the order reaches the market), and the missed-trade/opportunity cost (price move on the unfilled portion).
Because it is a single, all-in number expressed in basis points, IS is the preferred cost metric and the objective that execution algorithms try to minimize.
sections.formula:
IS = Paper return - Actual return
   = Exec cost + Delay cost + Missed-trade cost + Explicit costs

callout.label: SIGN
callout.text: IS is a cost: favorable price moves can make a component negative, lowering total shortfall.

body: Benchmarks judge whether a fill was good. VWAP weights each print by its volume; beating VWAP means you traded better than the average participant that day.

Arrival price (the midquote when the order hits the market) aligns closely with IS and rewards fast, low-impact execution. TWAP spreads a benchmark evenly over time, while closing price suits index funds marked at the close.
VWAP is easy to game (just trade with the volume) and can flatter a trader who simply delays, so it complements rather than replaces implementation shortfall.
sections.formula: VWAP = sum( Price_i x Volume_i ) / sum( Volume_i )

callout.label: PICK ONE
callout.text: Arrival-price/IS reward speed and low impact; VWAP rewards patience and blending with the crowd.

body: Modern markets are electronic order-driven systems where a central limit order book matches buyers and sellers by price-time priority. Traders supplying limit orders provide liquidity; those hitting them with market orders take it.
Quote-driven (dealer) markets, common in bonds and FX, rely on dealers posting two-way quotes. Brokered markets handle unique or illiquid assets via search.
Electronic venues added ECNs, alternative trading systems, and dark pools that hide size to reduce impact. Speed, low cost, and transparency improved, but so did complexity.

News traders profit from acting on information faster than others. Electronic dealers/market makers earn the spread by continuously quoting both sides. Arbitrageurs exploit price gaps across venues or related instruments.
Front runners detect large pending orders and trade ahead of them, and quote matchers (parasitic traders) piggyback on others' limit orders to capture a near-free option on price moves.
Many of these are high-frequency traders (HFT): automated strategies competing on latency, submitting and cancelling huge volumes of orders in microseconds.

callout.label: ROLE
callout.text: HFT market makers can tighten spreads; parasitic traders raise costs for slower participants.

body: Fragmentation spreads liquidity across dozens of venues. It can narrow spreads through competition but forces smart order routing and can worsen impact when depth is thin.
Systemic risks include runaway algorithms and feedback loops that can trigger flash crashes, so exchanges use circuit breakers and price limits.

Abusive practices to know: front running; spoofing/layering (fake orders to move price, then cancel); quote stuffing (flooding to slow rivals); gunning/pump-and-dump and bluffing to trigger stops; and wash trading to fake volume. All undermine market integrity and are illegal or restricted.

callout.label: SPOOFING
callout.text: Placing large orders with no intent to fill, to mislead price, is manipulation - not liquidity provision.

flow: Decision made at the decision (benchmark) price
Order routed - delay cost accrues before it reaches the market
Fills occur - spread, commissions, and market impact hit
Sum the components into implementation shortfall (bps)
Compare against VWAP/arrival-price benchmarks to grade execution

quiz.q: A manager decides to buy 1,000 shares when the price is $20.00. All 1,000 fill at an average of $20.10 with a $0.05/share commission. What is the implementation shortfall?
Trades print as 100 @ $10, 200 @ $11, and 200 @ $12. What is the VWAP?
Which cost is NOT an explicit trading cost?
quiz.e: Market impact is an implicit cost (adverse price movement from your own order). Commissions and fees are explicit and appear on the trade confirmation.

quiz.q: An order for 1,000 shares (decision price $50) fills 700 shares at $50.20 with $14 total commission; the rest goes unfilled and the price ends at $50.30. The $90 loss on the 300 unfilled shares represents which IS component?
quiz.e: 300 unfilled x ($50.30-$50.00) = $90 is the missed-trade/opportunity cost on shares that were never bought as the price ran away.

quiz.q: Why can VWAP be a misleading execution benchmark?
o: It ignores commissions entirely and cannot be computed intraday
A trader can beat it by simply delaying trades and blending with volume, and it rewards patience over urgency
quiz.e: VWAP is easy to game by trading in line with volume or delaying; it does not penalize opportunity cost the way implementation shortfall does.

quiz.q: Placing large limit orders with no intention of executing them to push the price, then cancelling, is best described as:
quiz.e: Spoofing/layering uses fake orders to create a false impression of supply/demand and is an abusive, illegal manipulation - not genuine liquidity provision.

quiz.q: Which trader type earns the bid-ask spread by continuously posting two-sided quotes?
quiz.e: Electronic dealers (market makers) supply liquidity by quoting both bid and ask, profiting from the spread. Front runners and news traders instead act on order flow or information.
